identity: Recognizable in 1 second by: near-black canvas (#010102, a black with a faint blue tint) + one lavender accent (#5e6ad2) + a razor-sharp product screenshot floating as the hero image. The single organizing idea: THE PRODUCT IS THE WEBSITE. Linear never illustrates what it does — it shows its actual UI, dense and real, on a dark stage. Everything else (copy, color, motion) is subtracted until only the interface and one sentence remain. Darkness reads premium, not gloomy, because it is treated as a luminance system: information density is managed through gradations of white opacity (4 text tints, 4 surface steps, 3 hairline tones) rather than added colors. Content emerges from the dark like a lit screen in a dark room — which is exactly the mood of its users at work.
anatomy: ~10 sections on the homepage: (1) Nav, 56px, canvas-colored, 6 primary links. (2) Hero: 8-word headline, 11-word sub, one CTA pair, then immediately a full fake-but-real issue view ('Faster app launch', ID 02/145, labels, priority, an agent participating in the activity feed) — the product IS the hero image. (3) Value-prop triptych: 'A new species of product tool' / 'Powered by agents' / 'Designed for speed' — each 1 heading + 1 sentence. (4-8) Five NUMBERED workflow chapters — 1.0 Intake 'Make product operations self-driving', 2.0 Plan 'Define the product direction', 3.0 Build 'Move work forward across teams and agents', 4.0 Review 'Review PRs and agent output', 5.0 Monitor 'Understand progress at scale' — each is one short heading + one dense UI artifact (a backlog, a roadmap timeline Feb–Sep, an agent terminal, a code diff, an analytics dashboard). The numbering turns the page into a product walkthrough with a table-of-contents feel. (9) Changelog strip: 4 dated recent updates — proof of velocity, no adjectives. (10) Social proof: 3 exec testimonials (OpenAI, Ramp, Opendoor) + '37,000 product teams' stat, then footer. Job distribution: 1 section sells the idea, 5 sections show the product, 2 sections prove momentum/trust. Marketing chrome is a minority of the page.
copyDiscipline: Hero H1: 'The product development system for teams and agents' — 8 words. Hero sub: 'Purpose-built for planning and building products. Designed for the AI era.' — 11 words, two sentences. Section headings run 4–7 words: 'Define the product direction' (4), 'Understand progress at scale' (4), 'Make product operations self-driving' (5), 'Review PRs and agent output' (5), 'Move work forward across teams and agents' (7). The house style is the 6-word twin-sentence aphorism: 'Plan the present. Build the future.' (6), 'Built for the future. Available today.' (6), 'A new species of product tool.' (6). Claims-to-proof ratio is roughly 1:1 — every abstract claim sits directly above a concrete artifact (a real-looking screenshot, a dated changelog entry, a named customer metric: 2.0x filed issues, 3.3x faster resolution, 28% issues authored by agents, '60% of Ramp's merged PRs'). Body copy under headings is one sentence, almost never two. How they say a lot with little: the screenshot carries the explanation, so the words only need to name the chapter; nouns over adjectives ('system', 'agents', 'issues' — almost no 'powerful/seamless/effortless'); numbers do the bragging. Three best lines verbatim: (1) 'Plan the present. Build the future.' (2) 'A new species of product tool.' (3) 'There is a lost art of building true quality software.' (Method page — a manifesto opener that positions the tool as a philosophy).
typography: Two families only: Linear's custom display/text sans (SF Pro Display fallback; site body historically Inter Variable with cv01/ss03 features) and Linear Mono (SF Mono fallback) for code/IDs. Weights are deliberately capped: display maxes at 600 — never 700+ — which is a big part of why the dark pages feel calm instead of shouty; signature body weight is ~510 (variable-font medium). Scale: 80px/600 hero with -3.0px tracking, 56px section openers (-1.8px), 40px subsections (-1.0px), 28px headlines, 16px body at 1.5 line-height, 13px/+0.4px eyebrows, 13px mono. Hierarchy is built three ways at once: size, negative tracking that scales with size (aggressive -3px at 80px tapering to 0 at body), and text COLOR tint (4 steps: #f7f8f8 → #d0d6e0 → #8a8f98 → #62666d). Tint hierarchy does most of the work — a card can have title/body/meta all at 14-16px and still read as three levels purely through white-opacity.
color: Astonishingly few colors for a whole site: 1 canvas (#010102), 4 surface steps (#0f1011 / #141516 / #18191a / #191a1b), 3 hairline border tones (#23252a / #34343a / #3e3e44), 4 text tints, ONE chromatic accent (#5e6ad2 lavender, hover #828fff) and one semantic green (#27a644, success only). Each color has exactly one job: lavender = brand mark, CTA, focus ring, link emphasis — never decoration; surfaces = elevation (higher surface number = closer/hovered/selected, replacing shadows entirely — 'No drop shadows' is a hard rule); hairlines = structure. Dark-vs-light strategy: total commitment to dark — there is no light marketing mode. Darkness is the native medium, not a theme. The reason it feels premium instead of gloomy: the black is slightly blue-tinted (screen-glow warm), the text is never pure white (no glare), and screenshots supply the brightness — the interface previews are the 'light source' of every section.
layout: 4px base spacing unit, 96px between sections — huge vertical air around dense artifacts, that alternation (breathing space / dense screenshot / breathing space) is the page's rhythm. Not a bento site: instead of grids of small feature tiles, each numbered chapter gets one FULL-WIDTH dense artifact; the only 3-up grid is the value-prop triptych. Radius ladder encodes object class: 8px buttons/inputs, 12px cards, 16px product screenshots, pill for toggles — you can identify what something is from its corner radius. Data display: real product tables and timelines shown at native density (issue IDs like '02/145' in mono, status dots, priority chips) rather than simplified marketing versions — density itself is the credibility signal. Numbers on the customers page are giant bare stats (2.0x / 3.3x / 28%) with a one-line label, no chart decoration. Card padding is tiered by importance: 24px feature/pricing cards, 32px testimonials, 48px CTA banners. Nav is a slim 56px bar that stays out of the way.
motion: Doctrine: motion demonstrates the product, never decorates the page. What moves (from teardowns of the site, incl. the frontendfyi rebuild): the hero UI assembles itself — issue rows, status changes and agent replies animate into the activity feed like a live session; the interactive keyboard-shortcut section presses real keys; the command-menu (Cmd+K) demo opens on interaction; screenshots fade/rise ~12-20px on scroll-entry with stagger, ease-out, fast (sub-400ms feel), settle and STOP — nothing loops. Hover states are near-instant (~150ms) surface-lift (surface-1 → surface-2) instead of scale or glow. Subtle radial gradient glows sit behind key artifacts as static atmosphere, not animation. What NEVER moves: the canvas/background, the type (no letter-by-letter reveals, no parallax text), the nav, and anything after it has entered — one entrance, then permanent stillness. The discipline is countable: per section, roughly one animated artifact, zero ambient loops.
proof: Five proof mechanisms, all artifact-based rather than adjective-based: (1) The product UI itself, shown dense and real — a fake screenshot this detailed (IDs, labels, agent activity) is the strongest 'this exists and works' signal. (2) One giant number, repeated site-wide: '37,000' (product teams / companies) — a single memorized stat instead of many small ones. (3) Named-customer metrics with the customer as the hero of the sentence: 'Boom Supersonic builds as fast as it flies', 'Why OpenAI chose Linear and scaled to 3,000 users', 'The coding agent behind 60% of Ramp's merged PRs' — case-study titles are stories, not logos. (4) The changelog on the homepage: 4 dated entries proving shipping velocity — momentum as trust. (5) The Method page: publishing your philosophy ('Practices for building') positions the company as an authority, so the tool inherits credibility. Testimonials are few (3 on the homepage) but from maximal names (OpenAI, Ramp, Opendoor), execs quoted on speed and quality. Nothing says 'trusted by' without a number or a name attached.
navFooter: Nav: 6 primary items (Product, Resources, Customers, Pricing, Now, Contact) + utility cluster (Docs, Open app, Log in, Sign up) — 'Open app' promoted to the nav because most visitors are existing users; the site is a front door, not a brochure. 56px tall, canvas-colored, no mega-visual dropdowns dominating. Footer is the inverse: deliberately dense, 6 columns ~37 links (Product 7, Features 8, Company 6+7 incl. Method/Quality/Brand — they link their own design philosophy pages, Resources 6-7 incl. Switch/Developers/Status, Connect 6, Legal 4). Promoted: app entry, docs, changelog ('Now'), customers. Buried: legal, brand assets. Pattern: minimal top (choices reduced to ~6), exhaustive bottom (SEO + power-user wayfinding).
weaknesses: (1) It spawned a genre — 'Linear design' is now the default SaaS look (dark canvas, glow, gradient, Inter, glassmorphism), so copying its surface is copying a thousand imitators; LogRocket's critique is blunt: 'almost every SaaS website looks the same'. Only the discipline transfers, not the aesthetic. (2) It only works because the product screenshots are gorgeous — the whole page delegates persuasion to UI imagery; a service business with no beautiful UI to show would have empty sections. (3) Assumes an in-crowd: 8-word headline 'The product development system for teams and agents' is meaningless to anyone who doesn't already know the category; near-zero explanation for genuine newcomers. (4) Dark-only excludes contexts where dark reads wrong (and there's no evidence dark converts better — it's a taste choice they can afford because their audience lives in dark IDEs). (5) Pricing page is the flattest page on the site — table + one stat, little of the craft of the homepage. (6) The 4-step gray-on-black text hierarchy runs close to accessibility contrast limits at the tertiary/quaternary tints (#62666d on #010102). (7) Very low information for evaluators in a hurry: no explainer video, no interactive demo without signup — confidence bordering on opacity.

site: ramp.com — corporate cards, spend management and AP automation platform (fintech, 70,000+ customers). Assigned lens: bento/grid discipline for number-dense content + how a finance company earns visual trust. Studied via live DOM inspection (computed styles, grid metrics, counter internals), not just fetched text.
pagesStudied: https://bakkenbaeck.com/case/ramp (agency case study on the 'Bento box' graphic system)
ramp.com llms/AI-optimized content (stats inventory: 70k businesses, 27M hours, 75% faster close)
identity: One organizing idea: A LIVE LEDGER. The site behaves like a financial instrument, not a brochure — the first thing you see is a ticking counter ("US CORPORATE PAYMENTS PROCESSED BY RAMP: 0.80%...") rolling in real time above the headline. Recognizable in 1 second by three signals: (1) near-monochrome warm ink-on-white with a single chartreuse (#E4F222) that appears ONLY on action, (2) one typeface (Lausanne) at one weight (400) at every size from 10px tickers to 64px display, (3) numbers everywhere, always paired with a name or a label. The brand says: we are calm, precise, and always running — trust is conveyed by the interface itself looking like accounting.
anatomy: ~12 sections, measured live: 1) HERO — 5-word headline, 12-word subtext, email field + CTA, and a live ticker strip of 9 rolling counters (AGENTS AT WORK TODAY, RECEIPTS PROCESSED, ACCOUNTING FIELDS CODED, INVOICES PROCESSED, TOTAL AI ACTIONS...). Job: prove the machine is running before making any claim. 2) SOCIAL-PROOF BAND — "Join 70,000 of the world's most ambitious companies growing 3.2x faster..." + "Read the report" link. 3) STAT CARD — giant "$1M+ / saved on global spend" at 64px. 4) PLATFORM OVERVIEW — heading + 5 one-line product links with arrow_outward icons (Cards & Expenses / Procure to pay / Accounting automation / Banking / 200+ Integrations). 5) PROBLEM VIZ — "Systems that never spoke" + "This is what five separate systems to reimburse a flight looks like" (canvas chaos diagram). 6) INTELLIGENCE PITCH — "Built on the intelligence of 70k+ finance teams." 7-9) THREE FEATURE+TESTIMONIAL PAIRS — each = 1 claim heading (28px) + 1 product link + 1 named quote with video (Stack/Specialized Accounting, Agents/Perplexity, Policy Agents/Valence). 10) DEMO CTA — "See what agents can automate." 11) ENTERPRISE — "Scale the team. Shrink the paperwork." + 2 capability cards. 12) TESTIMONIAL WALL — "70,000 teams and counting / We've got the receipts." ~18 short quotes. 13) BOOKEND CTA — the exact hero headline + email field repeated. Rhythm: claim → proof → claim → proof, never two claims in a row.
copyDiscipline: THE headline: "Time is money. Save both." — 5 words, two sentences, zero jargon. Subtext: "Cards, expenses, bill payments, and banking* – in the blink of AI." — 12 words (with a compliance asterisk even in the hero — finance honesty as style). Section headings counted: "Systems that never spoke" (4), "Scale the team. Shrink the paperwork." (6), "We've got the receipts." (4), "One platform for all of finance. Agents for every workflow, working 24/7." (13), "Built on the intelligence of 70k+ finance teams. One platform for the agentic era." (14). Body under headings is 1-2 sentences max; product features are single lines ("Banking that flows money to the highest return" — 8 words). Claims-to-proof ratio is roughly 1:1 — nearly every claim sits next to a counted number (70,000 / 3.2x / $1M+ / 200+ / 30+ currencies) or a named human (18+ testimonials, all with full name + exact title + company; quotes are 1-2 sentences). 3 best lines verbatim: (1) "Time is money. Save both." (2) "We've got the receipts." — a pun that is simultaneously the product, the proof, and the joke. (3) "You had a bureaucracy. Now you have a business again." Also elite: "This is what five separate systems to reimburse a flight looks like." — the problem stated as an exhibit, not an argument. Formula: aphorism headline (4-6 words) → mechanism subtext (8-14 words) → number or name. Never adjectives ("powerful", "seamless" are absent); verbs and nouns do the work.
typography: ONE typeface, ONE weight: Lausanne (custom neo-grotesque), font-weight 400 everywhere — measured on h1, h2, body, buttons. Hierarchy is built entirely from SIZE and SPACING, never boldness: h1 64px/64px line-height (1.0, ultra-tight), tracking -0.01px; section h2s at 48px/50px; sub-heads 40px/42px and 28px/32px; body 16px; ticker labels 10px UPPERCASE with +0.18px positive tracking and 60% opacity ink. Numbers use tabular-nums (verified in counter markup) so digits never jitter while rolling. A mono face exists only inside canvas data-graphics, not in copy. Lesson: single-weight + size-only hierarchy reads as engineered restraint — exactly the "calm accountant" register — but demands generous size jumps (10 → 16 → 28 → 48 → 64 is roughly a 1.7x ladder).
color: Counted from 3,000 live elements: effectively FOUR colors. (1) Ink: near-black warm charcoal (lab ~2.8, ≈#1D1C1B) — 2,733 of 3,000 elements; its 60% opacity version is the only "secondary text". (2) Canvas: pure white body with warm off-white card fill (lab 95.6, ≈#F1F0EE). (3) Hairline: rgba(33,33,33,0.1) — every border on the site is this one 10%-ink line. (4) Chartreuse #E4F222 — found on exactly 8 elements, ALL of them CTAs ("Get started for free", "See a demo", "Switch in days, not months"). One accent = one meaning = "act now". No blue, no gradient, no shadow color. A single dark slate block (rgb 43,46,53) for contrast sections. Dark-vs-light strategy: light is the default trust register (paper, ledger); dark is used sparingly as punctuation, never as a mode. Trust insight: a finance brand earns credibility by REFUSING color — when everything is ink-on-paper, the one green-yellow button reads as the single decision you're being asked to make.
layout: Measured grid facts: content column ~1137px inside 1280 viewport (~1200px max-width + padding). The bento signature is not "cards floating on a page" — it is ONE container, rounded 12px, overflow hidden, display:grid with **gap: 1px and a gray background**, so the gap itself paints hairline seams between cells (found live: 8-column grid, gap-px, bg-gray, rounded-[12px]). Cells are flat white/off-white, borderless, shadowless — the container's 1px seams do all the separation. Elsewhere: 2-col and 3-col grids with 24px gap (gap-6), stepping md:gap-10/lg:gap-16 on feature rows. Cards that stand alone: 12px radius, 1px rgba(33,33,33,0.1) border, box-shadow none — cards rest on borders, not shadows. Number display pattern (customers page): [logo] + [huge figure, 64px, tabular] + [outcome phrase ≤8 words, small] — e.g. "Barry's / 400 hours / back monthly from doing expense reports", "Glossier / 90% / of transactions automatically coded". The number is the headline; the words are the caption. Ticker pattern (hero): 10px uppercase label + value inside a subtle gray pill (rounded-sm, px-1.5). Pricing: 3 tiers each named with an AI-gradation label (AI-assisted / AI-powered / AI-tailored), then a full comparison table using only 3 glyph states (check_circle / remove_circle_outline / "+ explanatory sentence").
motion: Motion is CONFINED TO DATA AND MEDIA; layout and text never move. (1) Hero counters use number-flow (odometer digit-roll web component, found in DOM: <number-flow-react>, tabular-nums, aria-label with real value) — constant, quiet, incremental rolling; this is the site's heartbeat. (2) 7 canvases run ambient data animations (the Bakken & Baeck 'Bento box' system was explicitly built to host "high-density visuals — animations of multiple currency transactions"). (3) 3 inline videos inside testimonial cards, play-on-click. (4) Hover: a single global 0.3s transition on color/background/transform for links and buttons; arrows (arrow_forward/arrow_outward glyphs) nudge on hover. No scroll-jacking, no parallax, no entrance animations on text. Rule extracted: motion = evidence (numbers ticking, money moving), never decoration.
proof: Five stacked proof systems, zero bragging tone: (1) LIVE COUNTERS — 9 named operational metrics rolling in the hero; the machine proves itself before the copy speaks. (2) COUNTED CLAIMS — every scale claim is a specific number: 70,000 companies, 3.2x faster growth "than the average American business" (benchmarked, not vague), $1M+ saved, 200+ integrations, 30+ currencies. (3) NAMED HUMANS — 18+ testimonials on the homepage alone, every one with full name + exact title + company (CEO of Eventbrite, Controller of Perplexity, a small-town MAYOR — the range itself is the argument); quotes are specific and emotional, not corporate ("Before Ramp it was a process from the dark ages. We had people just doing expenses full-time. It was miserable."). (4) STAT WALL — customers page = logo + big number + outcome phrase, 20 companies, numbers first. (5) INSTITUTIONAL FINE PRINT — the footer carries full bank-issuer disclosures (Celtic Bank, Sutton Bank, FDIC, FCA reference numbers) and a support phone number; the asterisk in the hero subtext links to it. The compliance boilerplate is worn openly as a trust artifact. Header proof: "We've got the receipts" — proof reframed as the product itself.
navFooter: NAV: announcement bar (one rotating "New:" item) + 7 top-level items — Products, Partners, Solutions, Resources, Customers, Pricing + [Sign in, See a demo]. Demo CTA carries the chartreuse; everything else is ink. Mega-menus underneath are dense but the bar itself is minimal. FOOTER: 135 links (counted), organized in columns: Company (About/Careers), Products (16 links), Platform (10), Partners (8), Solutions (4 by company size), then a huge "Free tools and resources" block (~15 SEO calculators: savings calculator, per-diem calculator, charge finder, mission statement generator...) — the footer doubles as an SEO farm, deliberately buried below the fold of attention. Then legal/disclosure text (bank issuers, FDIC, FCA). Promoted: demo + email capture (appears 3x on homepage). Buried: everything speculative. The site bookends: final section repeats the hero headline + email field verbatim.
weaknesses: (1) 135 footer links is an SEO dump — visually orderly but useless to a human; do not copy the calculator farm. (2) The testimonial wall (~18 quotes, and the customers page literally renders its 20-item stat wall TWICE in the DOM for a marquee loop) overshoots; by quote 12 the reader is skimming. Second Shift needs 5-6 max. (3) Nine simultaneous hero counters is past the noise threshold — the labels blur together (AGENT INTERACTIONS vs TOTAL AI ACTIONS is double-counting); 3-4 counters would be stronger. (4) 10px labels at 60% opacity fail comfortable readability; the aesthetic wins over accessibility. (5) The 2026 AI-pivot copy ("agentic era", "blink of AI", AI-assisted/powered/tailored tiers) dates the site and muddies the once-crystal value prop of "save time and money" — trend-surfing dilutes an otherwise timeless voice. (6) Single-weight typography means no bold for inline emphasis; fine at display sizes, limiting in long-form. (7) "View Demo"/"Get started for free" repeats so often (6+ times) it borders on nagging. (8) Mega-menu density under a clean bar is a bait-and-switch — first click drops you into a 40-link panel.

site: anthropic.com (with claude.com/product/overview as the product-side satellite — Anthropic split the estate in two: anthropic.com = research institution, claude.com = product store)
pagesStudied: Supplementary teardowns: type.today/en/journal/anthropic, shadcn.io/design/anthropic, getdesign.md/claude/design-md, fontofweb.com/pin/1469
identity: Recognizable in 1 second as: a research journal printed on warm paper, not a tech site. The single organizing idea is INSTITUTIONAL CALM — the site behaves like a public institution publishing its record, not a company selling. Ivory paper (#FAF9F5), near-black slate ink (#141413), one serif voice + one sans voice, hand-drawn-ish geometric illustration, and a total absence of gradients, glassmorphism, dark-SaaS glow, or urgency. The logotype itself carries the whole brand: plain wordmark with a single slash. Confidence is communicated by refusing to decorate. Everything on the page is either a statement or a dated artifact — nothing is a pitch.
anatomy: The homepage is astonishingly short: 5 sections + footer. (1) HERO — one headline + one 24-word paragraph, no product screenshot, no CTA cluster; its job is to state the thesis. (2) PHILOSOPHY BAND — a single 6-word sentence ("Anthropic is built on hard questions.") + one supporting line + one "Learn more" button; job: tone-setting. (3) LATEST RELEASES — exactly 3 dated announcement cards (Opus 5, Sonnet 5, Claude Science), each one sentence long; job: prove momentum with timestamps. (4) FEATURED CONTENT — a 5-item grid of artifacts (Core views on AI safety, Responsible Scaling Policy, Academy, Economic Index, Claude's Constitution), each with a mono category tag; job: prove depth by pointing at the archive. (5) FOOTER — a massive 9-column sitemap. That's it. No testimonials, no logo wall, no pricing teaser, no feature grid on the homepage. Interior pages follow one template: hero statement → numbered content blocks (careers uses "01/07" section counters) → dated index table → single CTA ("Join us" / "See open roles"). The /news and /research pages are literally tables: Date | Category | Title rows with search — the densest information display on the site is a table of contents.
copyDiscipline: This is their superpower and exactly what the founder wants. COUNTS: Hero headline = 10 words ("AI research and products that put safety at the frontier"). Hero subtext = 24 words ("AI will have a vast impact on the world. Anthropic is a public benefit corporation dedicated to securing its benefits and mitigating its risks."). Section headings run 4-7 words: "Anthropic is built on hard questions." (6), "Making AI systems you can rely on" (7, company hero), "Shape how AI meets the world" (6, careers hero), "How we support you" (4), "How we hire" (3). Value names are 4-6 words: "Hold light and shade", "Do the simple thing that works", "Put the mission first". Release card copy = one sentence (~15-20 words). Claims-to-proof ratio is near 1:1 — almost every claim is immediately adjacent to a dated, clickable artifact (a policy, a paper, a release); they make no numeric boasts on the homepage at all (zero "10x faster", zero customer counts). How they say a lot with little: (a) sentences are declarative and end early; (b) the artifact does the persuading, the copy just points; (c) they use candor as compression — careers page: "About half our technical staff had no prior ML experience; about half have PhDs, but plenty of brilliant colleagues never went to college." — a trust-building paragraph that no benefits list could match. THREE BEST LINES VERBATIM: 1) "Anthropic is built on hard questions." 2) "Making AI systems you can rely on" 3) "Hold light and shade". (Honorable mention from claude.com: "Meet your thinking partner" — 4 words.)
typography: Two faces, strict division of labor: Styrene (A wide/geometric + B narrow, by Berton Hasebe) for headlines, nav, UI, labels; Tiempos Text (Klim) for body prose. The signature move is the DUAL DISPLAY SYSTEM: sans weight 700 (~61px) for declarative statements vs serif weight 400 (~68px) for editorial/reflective statements — same size class, opposite temperament, often mixed within one page or even one headline. Third voice: uppercase mono-style small caps for category tags, dates, and section counters ("01/07") — the structural metadata layer. Hierarchy is built almost entirely from face-switching and generous size jumps, not from weight ladders or color; body text stays one size, one weight, comfortable measure (~65-75ch). Result: three distinct voices (declare / reflect / annotate) with only ~4 total styles.
color: Radically restrained warm-only system: ivory canvas #FAF9F5, slate ink #141413, mid gray #B0AEA5, light warm gray #E8E6DC for card surfaces, and ONE hero accent — clay/"book cloth" #D97757 — used for the logo slash, links, and small highlights only. A secondary accent set exists (sky #6A9BCC, olive #788C5D, fig #C46686, cactus #BCD1CA) but is SCOPED: only research sub-pages and data viz get them; the homepage never does. Zero cool grays, zero blues in the core UI, zero gradients. Dark-vs-light strategy: there is no dark mode marketing site at all — dark is what everyone else does; paper is the differentiation. Depth is conveyed by surface-tone shifts (ivory → warm gray) plus 24px radii, never shadows — the "stacked paper" effect. Deliberate positioning: distinct from OpenAI's clinical whites/blues and enterprise-AI dark gradients.
layout: Editorial single-column spine with occasional card grids — no bento walls. Cards appear in exactly two shapes: the 3-across dated release card and the content-index card with image + mono tag + title + date. The most distinctive layout pattern is the INDEX TABLE: /news and /research present dozens of items as spreadsheet-calm rows (Date | Category tag | Title, no descriptions), searchable, paginated with a plain "See more". Numbers/data are almost never displayed in marketing chrome — data lives inside linked research artifacts (Economic Index) where it gets the full accent palette. Numbered structure everywhere: 7 numbered values, "01/07" section counters, 5 named teams. Whitespace is the grid: sections are separated by huge vertical gaps rather than background stripes. 24px radius on every card-level surface, consistent, doing the softening work that shadows do elsewhere.
motion: Doctrine of stillness. Per teardowns of their own bundled frontend-design guidance: "one well-orchestrated page load with staggered reveals (animation-delay)" instead of scattered micro-interactions — the page enters once, in sequence, then stops. What moves: initial staggered fade/rise on load, link underline/color hovers, gentle card hover lifts, the occasional subtly-animated geometric illustration. What NEVER moves: no scroll-jacking, no parallax, no auto-playing carousels, no counters, no background particles, no cursor effects, no marquee logo strips. Body text and tables never animate. The stillness IS the message — a site about safety that fidgets would contradict itself.
proof: Credibility without bragging, four mechanisms: (1) PROOF-BY-ARTIFACT — instead of claims, dated clickable documents: Responsible Scaling Policy, Claude's Constitution, Economic Index, a searchable publications table going back years. The archive is the testimonial. (2) TIMESTAMPS EVERYWHERE — every card and row carries a date; recency and volume are self-evident, never stated ("we publish a lot" is shown, not said). (3) STRUCTURAL PROOF — PBC status, board and Long-Term Benefit Trust listed by name on /company; governance as trust signal. (4) CANDOR — careers page openly states no internships, no feedback given, 12-month reapply rule, scam warnings, an AI-use-in-applications policy; admitting limits reads as honesty and transfers to everything else. Notably ABSENT from anthropic.com: customer logo walls, star ratings, testimonial quotes, vanity metrics — all pushed to claude.com. The homepage earns trust with zero social proof.
navFooter: Extreme asymmetry: nav is 5 items + 1 CTA (Research, Policy, Commitments, Learn, News | Try Claude) — note Research is FIRST and product is only the CTA button; the nav is a statement of priorities. Footer is a monster ~9-column sitemap (Products, Models, Solutions, Claude Platform, Resources, Programs, Company, Help/Security, Terms & Policies) holding 60+ links. The pattern: promote 5 ideas, bury everything else in the footer where committed users find it. Interior pages end with one single-sentence CTA band ("Want to help us build the future of safe AI? Join us") — one action per page, never a CTA zoo.
weaknesses: Honest minuses: (1) The homepage tells a first-time buyer almost nothing actionable — no what-it-costs, no how-it-works; Anthropic can afford that fame-subsidized vagueness, a marketplace cannot. Copy this structure without their brand equity and you get a beautiful page that doesn't convert. (2) The anthropic.com/claude.com split is confusing — /claude 301s to another domain with a different nav, different tone ("Meet your thinking partner" is markedly weaker/vaguer copy than the mothership's). (3) Footer overload: 60+ links, several near-duplicate columns (Resources vs Learn vs Programs) — the "bury it" strategy has tipped into landfill. (4) Index tables with no descriptions force a click to know if an item matters. (5) CTAs are so understated (quiet text buttons) that conversion paths are easy to miss entirely. (6) The claude.com product page slips back into generic SaaS patterns (tabbed feature demos, "Explore X" buttons) — proof that the editorial system strains when it must actually sell features. (7) Sameness risk: Claude's own bundled design skills now stamp this aesthetic onto thousands of generated sites; the look is being commoditized, so copying its surface (ivory + serif) is already a cliché — only the underlying discipline is worth stealing.

pagesStudied: Supplement: VoltAgent/awesome-design-md Notion DESIGN.md token teardown, designmd/getdesign.md analyses, Mobbin brand palette
identity: The one-second tell: the marketing site looks like a Notion page. Warm paper-white canvas (#f6f5f4 sections on #ffffff), warm-charcoal ink (#37352f family, never cold gray), one signature purple CTA (#5645d4), soft 12px-radius cards, and real product screenshots floating on deep shadows. The single organizing idea is SELF-DEMONSTRATION: the product's own aesthetic (blocks, database-tag pastels, hand-drawn human illustrations) IS the brand system, so every marketing surface doubles as a product demo. Playfulness is kept credible for business buyers by strict containment — the whimsy lives only in illustrations and pastel card tints; the type, grid, buttons, and numbers are ruthlessly disciplined. Note: the 2026 site has tilted noticeably toward AI-enterprise seriousness (navy hero band #0a1530, agent-speak); the illustrated warmth now survives mostly on /about and in card tints.
anatomy: Homepage = 9 sections + nav + footer. (1) HERO: centered headline + 14-word subtext + dual CTA + animated pile of 7 workspace screenshots — the product is the hero image. (2) LOGO BAR: one line of proof ("Trusted by 98% of the Forbes Cloud 100") + 9 logos (OpenAI, Figma, Ramp, Cursor, Vercel, Clay, Remote, Faire, Toyota) + video play button. (3) CUSTOM AGENTS: ~150-word section with a 4-tile grid (Q&A / Task routing / Reporting / Create your own, ~15 words each). (4) NOTION AGENT: 9-word promise + two side-by-side screenshots. (5) ENTERPRISE SEARCH: 4-word promise + one screenshot. (6) AI MEETING NOTES: 4-word promise + one screenshot. (7) BRING WORK TOGETHER: trio of sub-features (Docs / Knowledge Base / Projects), each a product-noun label + one-line promise + screenshot. (8) TESTIMONIALS: ~120 words total across 5-7 customer cards, each = logo + quote + link. (9) STAT ROW: 7 countable numbers in a band. Pattern to memorize: every feature section is exactly [product noun] + [≤10-word promise] + [screenshot], repeated with metronomic regularity. Sections sit in a 1280px container with 64–96px vertical rhythm.
copyDiscipline: This is Notion's masterclass. HERO HEADLINE: "Where teams and agents Think together." — 6 words. HERO SUBTEXT: "Capture context, find answers, and automate tasks with AI built for your team." — 14 words, three verb phrases. SECTION HEADINGS (counted): "One search for everything." (4), "Perfect notes, every time." (4), "Less tracking. More progress." (4), "You assign the tasks. Notion Agent does the work." (9), "Simple and powerful" (3), "Knowledge and work. Connected." (4, enterprise hero). Feature tiles run ~10-15 words each; the whole homepage carries maybe 600 words of marketing copy against ~10 product screenshots. THE MECHANISM: (a) the two-beat sentence — a short declarative pair where sentence 1 names the pain-side and sentence 2 names the win ("Less tracking. More progress." / "You assign the tasks. Notion Agent does the work."); (b) headings never contain adjectives about the company, only outcomes for the reader; (c) every claim is immediately adjacent to a proof artifact (screenshot or number), so the copy doesn't have to argue. Claims-to-proof ratio is roughly 1:1 — for every promise there is a screenshot, a logo, or a counted stat. THREE BEST LINES VERBATIM: 1. "You assign the tasks. Notion Agent does the work." 2. "Less tracking. More progress." 3. "There's power in a single platform where you can do all your work. Notion is that single place." (OpenAI testimonial — note even the quote is two beats). Pricing plan descriptions are equally tight: "Essentials for staying organized." / "The AI workspace for work that matters."
typography: One family, three weights, zero exceptions. Notion Sans (an Inter-based custom cut) with system fallbacks; weights 400/500/600 only — no 700+, boldness comes from size. Scale: hero-display 80px/600/1.05 leading/-2px tracking → display 56px → H1 48px → H2 36px → H3 28px → subtitle 18px/400 → body 16px/400/1.55 → captions 13px → micro-uppercase 11px/600/+1px tracking. The trick: display sizes get TIGHT leading (1.05) and negative tracking for punch; body gets GENEROUS leading (1.55) for doc-like readability — the contrast between the two is the hierarchy. Hierarchy is built purely with size + weight + warm-gray text steps (#1a1a1a → #5d5b54 → #787671 → #a4a097), never with color. Micro-uppercase labels (11px, letterspaced) serve as section kickers. Third-party analyses mention 'serif headings' in Notion's warm-minimalism era; the current live site is effectively all-sans.
color: A strict three-tier system. TIER 1 — warm neutrals do 90% of the work: canvas #ffffff, section surface #f6f5f4, hairlines #e5e3df, ink #1a1a1a with warm-charcoal #37352f (the famous Notion text color — warm, not cold). TIER 2 — exactly one action color: purple #5645d4 owns every primary CTA sitewide; links get one blue #0075de; nothing else is clickable-colored. TIER 3 — contained decoration: 9 pastel card tints (peach #ffe8d4, rose #fde0ec, mint #d9f3e1, lavender #e6e0f5, sky #dcecfa, yellow #fef7d6...) that deliberately echo the product's own database-tag colors — decoration derived from the product, not invented; plus a navy hero band #0a1530 for the AI-era dark moment. Semantic: green #1aae39 success, orange #dd5b00 warning, red #e03131 error — used only functionally. Dark-vs-light strategy: light is the default identity; dark appears as a single framed hero band, never as a full page — dark is an accent, not a mode.
layout: 1280px max container, 32px gutters, 4px base grid. Universal 12px card radius (buttons 8px — rectangular, never pills), 1px hairline borders as the default card treatment with shadow reserved for elevation meaning: flat card = border only; feature card = 4px/12px soft shadow; product screenshot = deep 24px/48px 'mockup shadow' that makes screenshots feel like physical objects sitting on the page. Rhythm: centered hero (atypical for B2B), then alternating full-width feature sections, each one screenshot + short copy block; bento appears only in the agent-tile grid (4-up) and testimonial wall. Pricing is a clean 4-column card row with the recommended plan flagged by a 2px purple border + tinted background — highlight by border, not by size. Numbers are displayed in a dedicated stat band (#f6f5f4, 12px radius, 48px padding): big numeral + tiny label, 7-up. Data is never in tables on marketing pages except the pricing comparison table.
motion: Restraint as policy. What moves: the hero's animated pile of workspace screenshots (the one theatrical moment), inline product demo videos behind a play button, hover states (150–200ms ease — subtle elevation/tint shifts on cards, pressed-state color steps on buttons #5645d4→#4534b3), and scroll-triggered screenshot reveals. What NEVER moves: text, headlines, logos, nav, pricing numbers. Teardowns describe the site as 'live demos and animated transitions' but the animation budget is concentrated entirely on PRODUCT imagery — motion is used to prove the product is alive, never to decorate the page. No parallax, no scroll-jacking, no ambient particles. Caveat: static fetching limits verification here; treat these as the confirmed floor of their motion system.
proof: Numbers-first, adjectives-last. The signature move is the HYPER-SPECIFIC STAT: "98% of the Forbes Cloud 100" — weirder and more credible than "trusted by thousands." The full battery: 100M users, 62% of Fortune 100, 50%+ of YC companies, 1.4M community members, "#1 knowledge base 3 years running (G2)" ×3 categories. Logo strategy is curated for the moment: OpenAI, Cursor, Vercel, Clay — the AI-era darlings — signaling 'the companies you admire chose us.' Customer stories are packaged as editorial headlines with ONE metric each: "The Digital Double: How Baseten Scaled Its Most-Asked Expert — 5-10x the number of questions asked daily"; "Clay's New Default — 80+ active custom agents." Testimonial quotes are chosen for brevity and two-beat rhythm. And the deepest proof is structural: every feature claim sits beside a real product screenshot — the artifact IS the argument. Nothing on the site says "best" without a G2 attribution attached.
navFooter: Nav: three mega-menu groups (Product: 10 items led by AI/Agents; Solutions: by team, company size, use case; Resources: 11 items) plus flat top-level Developers / Enterprise / Pricing. Persistent dual CTA in the header — "Request a demo" (secondary) + "Get Notion free" (primary purple) — serving both self-serve and sales-led motions simultaneously. Promoted: AI features (top of every menu), Enterprise, Pricing. Buried: templates, community, academy (Resources). Footer: 5 columns (Company / Download / Resources / Notion For / social), a 20-language selector, app-download links given a whole column (product-led signal), hairline-separated, warm-charcoal text on white — quiet, dense, utilitarian. No footer CTA banner spam; the last conversion push is a dedicated pre-footer CTA band ("cta-banner-light" on #f6f5f4).
weaknesses: (1) Identity drift: the 2026 AI pivot ("Where teams and agents Think together" — with its awkward mid-sentence capital T gimmick) trades the beloved plain-language clarity for agent-buzzword fog; the hero headline is the weakest line on the site. (2) Enterprise page bloat: 18 sections with near-duplicate headings ("All-in-one AI, right where you work" / "One AI tool for everything" / "AI with all the right context" say the same thing three times) — the copy discipline of the homepage collapses under stakeholder pressure. Do not copy multi-section sprawl. (3) Pastel sprawl: 9 card tints is 6 too many; on dense pages the tints stop meaning anything. (4) Unattainable-logo proof: every testimonial is OpenAI/Toyota/Ramp scale — a small-business visitor finds nobody like themselves. (5) The /about page's lovely illustrated essay is orphaned — its warmth no longer matches the AI-corporate homepage, proof that maintaining two tones without a structural device (like Second Shift's seam/toggle) causes drift. (6) The illustrated identity that made Notion famous is now mostly gone from the money pages — they are coasting on residual brand memory.

site: stripe.com — assigned role: PRICING CLARITY + TECHNICAL CREDIBILITY (the reference for explaining money mechanics and being trusted to hold money)
pagesStudied: Supplementary teardowns: bram.us gradient breakdown (WebGL minigl), designmd/open-design/shadcn design-token extractions (sohne-var typography, indigo accent system)
identity: Recognizable in 1 second by ONE element: the animated pastel-to-indigo gradient band occupying the upper third of nearly every marketing page (cream → sherbet orange → lavender → electric indigo → ruby pink), with bold low-weight typography knocked out over it. The organizing idea is a single word: INFRASTRUCTURE. Not "payments app" — "Financial infrastructure to grow your revenue." Everything follows from that framing: the site looks and reads like a utility company for money — calm, numeric, exhaustively documented, never salesy. The gradient is the only expressive element they allow themselves; everything else is near-monochrome navy-on-cool-white restraint. That tension (one wild band of color + total discipline everywhere else) IS the brand. Second Shift's equivalent single organizing idea should be THE SEAM — the night/paper boundary doing the job Stripe's gradient does: the one place identity is allowed to be loud.
anatomy: Homepage is LONG — roughly 31 distinct sections, but they resolve into 9 bands, each with one job: (1) HERO: gradient canvas + 6-word headline + 18-word subtext + email-capture "Get started" — job: state the category. (2) SCALE TICKER: "global GDP running on Stripe" stat strip — job: instant scale proof before any feature. (3) PRODUCT BENTO (≈6 sections): "Flexible solutions for every business model" — payments, billing, issuing, crypto, Connect, each a card with a real product UI mockup (e.g. a "Pro Plan $0.01/1000 units" pricing card rendered as imagery) — job: show breadth via artifacts, not adjectives. (4) STATS BAND: "The backbone of global commerce" — US$1.9tn volume, 99.999% uptime, 135+ currencies, 200M+ subscriptions — job: quantify the claim made in band 2. (5) ENTERPRISE TRACK: 4 case studies (Hertz, URBN, Instacart, Le Monde), each one sentence + 2 stats + photo — job: de-risk for big buyers. (6) STARTUP TRACK: 8 one-line startup stories (Lovable, Supabase, Linear, ElevenLabs…) + Atlas + Startups programme — job: same de-risking for the other audience; note the site serves TWO audiences by sequencing bands, not by toggle. (7) PLATFORM/SaaS TRACK: 3 short benefit sections + 4 testimonial quotes. (8) DEVELOPER BAND: "Reliable, extensible infrastructure for every stack" — 500M+ API req/day, 10K+ req/sec, three integration paths — job: technical credibility as a closing argument. (9) NEWS GRID (8 cards) + Book of the week + final CTA. Pricing page is 7 sections: hero with exactly TWO tiers (Standard vs Custom), an out-of-the-box features list (8 items included free), anchor-tab nav (Standard / Custom / FAQs), per-product fee tables, enterprise logos, 5-question FAQ.
copyDiscipline: This is Stripe's masterclass. COUNTS: hero headline = 6 words ("Financial infrastructure to grow your revenue."). Hero subtext = 18 words. Pricing headline = 7 words ("Pricing built for businesses of all sizes"). Section headings run 3–6 words, verb-first, benefit-shaped: "Convert more customers" (3), "Less fraud, more revenue" (4), "Scale with confidence" (3), "Enable any billing model" (4), "Global reach, local experience" (4), "Embed payments in your platform" (5). Subtext under any heading is capped at 1–2 sentences, and that sentence almost always carries a NUMBER. Claims-to-proof ratio is effectively 1:1 — nearly every claim is welded to a countable stat: "Boost authorisation rates by 2.2% on average", "11.9% average revenue uplift", "99.999% historical uptime", "100% PCI audit success rate". Case studies are one sentence + two stats, formula: "[Customer] does [specific thing] with Stripe" ("URBN consolidates $5 billion in online and in-store revenue onto Stripe." — then "5+ consumer brands / 700+ store locations"). Adjectives are nearly absent; numbers do the persuading. THE 3 BEST LINES VERBATIM: (1) "from your first transaction to your billionth." — ambition + scale + you-focus in 7 words, no adjective. (2) "No setup fees, monthly fees, or hidden fees." — pricing trust as a triple negative, 8 words, sits directly under the price. (3) "2.9% + CA$0.30 per successful transaction" — the entire business model as one arithmetic expression; note "successful": you only pay when it works, one word carrying an entire guarantee. The lesson for the founder: Stripe says a lot with little by making every sentence do one of exactly two jobs — name a benefit (≤6 words) or prove it (a number). Nothing else survives.
typography: One family for everything: Söhne (sohne-var, variable). Radical move: weight 300 (light) even at 56px display sizes — reads as confident restraint instead of corporate shouting. Hierarchy is built through SIZE + TRACKING, not weight: display 32–56px with aggressive negative letter-spacing (-0.64px to -1.4px, e.g. 48px/-0.96px, line-height 1.15); body 15–18px at 0 tracking; captions/labels smaller with slight tightening. Critical for a money company: numerics use OpenType tabular figures (tnum) with -0.36 to -0.42px tracking so every fee table and stat column aligns like an instrument panel — prices never wiggle. Code and inline technical strings (`stripe docs`, version numbers like "v1.43.3+") appear in mono, which is exactly the Geist Mono structural-string role Second Shift already planned. No decorative or secondary display face anywhere.
color: Near-monochrome plus one earner: cool-white canvas (#fff → #f8fafd → #e5edf5 tint steps), deep navy (#0d253d family) for ALL text and dark surfaces, and ONE vivid indigo (#635bff/#533afd) that must earn its use — one filled CTA pill per band, links, icon strokes, nothing else. The famous multicolor gradient is quarantined to hero/atmosphere bands; it never touches UI components, tables, or pricing. Depth strategy is background tint-shift between sections rather than heavy borders; when shadows appear they're the signature blue-tinted rgba(50,50,93,0.25) stack, cool and atmospheric, never gray mud. Dark surfaces exist as CONTENT (dashboard mockups, the featured pricing tier, code panels) inside a light site — dark is used to frame the product, not as a site theme. Total functional palette: ~4 roles (canvas, ink, one accent, one atmosphere). This maps 1:1 to Second Shift's plan: night #0A0B0D and paper #F7F6F3 as the two canvases, green as the single earner (money only), the seam as the quarantined atmosphere.
layout: 12-col grid, content max-width ~1080px, generous side margins. Signature structural move: diagonally sheared section boundaries (skewY on band backgrounds) so sections interlock instead of stacking as flat stripes — the page reads as one continuous surface with angled color changes. Product breadth is handled as a bento grid of cards where each card contains a REAL rendered artifact (a checkout form, a Terminal device, a pricing card, a dashboard chart) — never abstract illustration. Numbers are displayed as instrument clusters: 3-up stat callouts (big tnum figure + 2–4 word label underneath, e.g. "500M+ / API requests per day"). Pricing page discipline: exactly 2 tiers side-by-side (Standard/Custom) — not 3, not 4 — then depth pushed into per-product fee tables below anchor tabs, so the top of the page stays one glance simple and the bottom rewards scrutiny. Case studies: photo + one-sentence claim + two-stat pair, identical card anatomy repeated, which makes 12 case studies scannable instead of exhausting. Buttons small, pill/4px radius, never oversized.
motion: Extremely rationed. What moves: (1) the hero gradient — a WebGL canvas (their custom "minigl" + Gradient class) with slow fluid color drift, and it's performance-disciplined: a ScrollObserver kills the animation the moment it leaves the viewport; (2) nav mega-menu panels morph/slide between dropdown states rather than popping; (3) light hover states on cards and links; (4) an occasional rotating globe/ticker in stats bands. What NEVER moves: prices, fee tables, numbers, body text, case-study cards, the docs — anything you'd need to trust or read is static. The rule extractable here: motion is allowed only in the identity layer (atmosphere) and the wayfinding layer (nav), never in the evidence layer (money, stats, tables). Scroll-triggered showmanship is absent; the page does not animate itself into your attention.
proof: Stripe never says "trust us"; it deposits evidence. Five mechanisms: (1) SCALE NUMBERS stated flatly — "Businesses on Stripe generated US$1.9tn in 2025", "50% of Fortune 100 companies have used Stripe", "> 90% chance that a card has been seen on Stripe at least once" (that last one is genius: network effect as a probability). (2) RELIABILITY AS SPEC SHEET — "99.999% historical uptime", "500M+ API requests per day", "US$40bn processed on BFCM at 99.9999%" — infrastructure metrics presented like an SLA, not marketing. (3) LOGOS stratified by audience: Amazon/BMW/Maersk for enterprise, Lovable/Supabase/Linear for startups — each band shows the logos its reader resembles. (4) ARTIFACTS: real checkout UIs, real dashboard screenshots, real fee arithmetic — the product itself is the imagery, implying "nothing to hide". (5) DOCUMENTATION DEPTH as competence signal: docs are a first-class marketing surface (linked from pricing tables via "Learn more"), with CLI access (`stripe docs`), versioned changelogs, API status page — the sheer maintained depth says "adults run this." Compliance is named specifically (PCI Level 1, "100% PCI audit success rate", regulatory licences), and third-party validation appears once (Forrester: 326% ROI) rather than as a wall of badges.
navFooter: Top nav is 5 items only — Products, Solutions, Developers, Resources, Pricing — plus Sign in and two CTAs (Start now / Contact sales). Pricing is promoted to top level; that placement is itself a trust statement (nothing to hide about money). All breadth lives in mega-menu dropdowns, keeping the bar minimal. The footer is the opposite: a deliberate CATALOGUE of ~80 links in 7 columns (26 products, 22 solutions, developer resources, integrations, resources, company, support) — the footer functions as the sitemap and as an SEO/credibility artifact: the sheer enumerated surface area says "this is a big, real system." Promoted: pricing, docs, contact sales. Buried: legal, licences, prohibited businesses (present but quiet — notable that they list "Prohibited businesses" at all; a merchant-of-record transparency move worth copying). Locale selector in footer signals global operation.
weaknesses: (1) The homepage is objectively bloated — 31 sections trying to serve enterprise, startup, SaaS-platform and developer audiences in one scroll; by band 20 the structure repeats itself (another track, another case-study set). Second Shift's two-audience toggle is a better answer than Stripe's sequential mega-scroll. (2) Product sprawl leaks into copy: jargon like "agentic commerce", "borderless money movement", "financial operating system" assumes the reader already speaks Stripe — at Second Shift's stage this vocabulary-building is unaffordable. (3) Weight-300 type at small sizes on tinted backgrounds skirts contrast/accessibility limits — do not copy light weights for body text on dark night backgrounds. (4) The WebGL gradient is expensive (custom minigl engine); a small team should get the same effect with CSS. (5) Some product-card imagery is inscrutable out of context (a floating "Pro Plan $0.01/1000 units" card means nothing to a non-customer). (6) The pricing page's localized quirks (CA$ amounts, "Starting at CA$770.00 per month, 1-year contract" appearing mid-page) briefly break the "simple, no hidden fees" promise the hero just made — the enterprise-priced products muddy the clean 2-tier story. (7) An 80-link footer only works when you genuinely have 26 products; copied prematurely it reads as fake scale.
